html:
A Muslim trading kingdom on the northwest coast of Java, founded in the 16th century, which grew rich exporting pepper. Its port city, called Bantam by Europeans, was one of the great markets of Southeast Asia in the late 1500s and 1600s.

Forces of the Demak Sultanate took the port from the Hindu kingdom of Sunda in the 1520s. Tradition names Sunan Gunungjati and his son Hasanuddin as the founders. The sultans controlled pepper from west Java and south Sumatra and drew traders from China, India, Arabia and Europe. The first Dutch fleet came here in 1596, and the English East India Company opened a trading post in 1602.

Banten lost ground once the Dutch founded Batavia nearby in 1619. Sultan Ageng Tirtayasa, who ruled from 1651 to 1683, fought hard to stay independent, but his son, known as Sultan Haji, called in the Dutch East India Company against him. In return the Company got a pepper monopoly and expelled the English. The sultans lived on as Dutch clients until Governor General Daendels and then the British abolished the sultanate in the early 19th century. See also the Bantam ship-deck market and pepper.
